Chapter 3: Building Trust and Leading with Integrity
Trust—it's such a fragile thing, isn’t it? It takes a long time to build, but can slip away in a heartbeat. In business, where deals come and go every single day, trust might seem like a luxury.
But if you’re aiming to lead, trust is the bedrock. Everything else? It rests right on top of it.
I want you to picture this: A leader, suddenly responsible for a big division, finds themselves in a tough spot. Their partner company made a mistake—a real one, and the fallout could hit both sides pretty hard. Now, it would've been easy to just shift the blame, play it safe, and protect the company at all costs. But there was something more important on the line: the relationship itself.
So, instead of pointing fingers, the leader picked up the phone, reached out, and said, “Here’s the problem. Let’s fix it together.” It wasn’t about being soft or dodging conflict. It was about seeing that real, lasting success depends on trust. And sometimes, integrity means choosing the harder path—doing the right thing, even when nobody's watching.
Funny thing is, most people don’t notice those little moments when trust is either built or chipped away. But over time, all those moments? They add up.
And it’s not just about deals with other companies. Inside the company, the same rules apply. Employees? They’re always watching. They take their cues from what leaders say—and what they do. When things go wrong, how leaders react really matters.
Leaders who own up to their mistakes, who can honestly say “I don’t know,” earn real respect. But if someone always acts like they have all the answers or punishes people for honest mistakes, you get a culture of fear. And in that kind of place, folks stay silent.
I’ll give you an example. One afternoon, a team member came forward with a tough issue. It was the kind of moment that could make any leader go on the defensive. But instead, the leader listened, thanked the person for their honesty, and they tackled the problem together.
And you know what? People are way more likely to speak up if they know they’ll be treated fairly. Over time, that openness led to smarter decisions—and way fewer surprises down the line.
As the company faced new challenges—competition ramping up, tech changing fast, customers wanting different things—trust became even more important. Both partners and employees needed to believe their leaders would act with integrity, even when it wasn’t convenient or easy.
Every little decision, every single day, became a chance to either strengthen or weaken that trust.
There were times when doing the right thing had a real cost. Like, imagine walking away from a lucrative deal because the terms just didn’t feel right. That’s not easy. But it sends a clear message: some things matter more than a quick win.
Most people never see the calculations behind tough choices like these. But they feel the effects in the culture—the sense that, here, we do things the right way.
Looking back, one thing stands out: trust and integrity aren’t just good values, they’re smart strategies. Companies that put them first attract better partners, keep their best people, and make it through tough times with their heads held high.
So, here’s the big takeaway: treat people with fairness and respect, and the rest? It usually takes care of itself.
